claims: Jev does not write text or code; it only makes decisions (yes/no, pick one, score 1-10) in a fraction of a second at a fraction of the cost
The slow part of an agent is often the big model deciding what you want, not the task itself
Codex connected Jev 'in one go' from the API key and docs
Each incoming message is first classified by Jev: task type, urgency, which model should handle it, in under a second
On screen: round-trip time 768.87 ms; routing decision in 0.70s with 100% task confidence
how_to_steps: Get a Jev API key from TypeSafe and put it in .env
Give Codex the key and the Jev docs and say 'connect this'
Codex creates a local Python MCP server exposing jev_decide (choice, yes/no, score) and registers it as a project MCP tool; restart Codex to load it
On each incoming message, call Jev with three questions: task type (spreadsheet/writing/research/code/other), urgent? (yes/no), model tier (fast/standard/heavy)
Route the message to the model/agent based on the answers; Codex then does the reasoning, writing and actions
on_screen_only: TypeSafe blog: 'We Took The Opposite Research Direction'

TypeSafe docs 'TypeSafe primitives': Choice (choose an option from a list -> choice, probabilities, confidence), Score (score the state on a rubric -> score, probabilities, confidence), Nous (is this statement true? -> nous [0-1]); 'All three question types can be mixed in a single API call. Every question is evaluated in parallel and in isolation against the same state in one go. Adding questions barely changes the response time. Each question is evaluated independently, so adding more questions does not create context-rot.' Heading 'Atomic questions, composed in code'

relevance.why: A fast pre-classifier that routes tasks to cheap vs heavy models is a sound pattern for any agent product a founder ships (cost and latency), and the MCP-tool wiring maps directly onto Claude Code.

implement_score.why: A half-day experiment: build the same jev_decide-style MCP tool (or do it with Claude Haiku + JSON schema) and use it to triage inbound tasks/emails before Opus/Sonnet. Only adopt Jev itself if it beats Haiku on cost/latency.

verify: TypeSafe AI / Jev availability, pricing per call, SDK and MCP support
Does 'in under a second' hold under load, and is the confidence calibrated?
Compare against a Haiku-class model with structured output before adding a dependency
Model names GPT-6-Astra / GPT-5.6-Sol are shown in a custom router UI; confirm they are real OpenAI models
